{"id": "7:24/q16", "question": "What do reports about snakes imply for people?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:24/q16/p1", "position": "Snakes should not be spared out of fear of their revenge; a persistent house snake may be killed after warning.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya reports Aisha's curse on one who leaves a snake for fear of revenge and Ibn Umar's assertion that one who leaves snakes alone is outside the community. A Prophetic report says Medina's jinn include Muslims, so warn a house snake three times; if it stays, kill it as an unbeliever."}]}
{"id": "7:24/q17", "question": "What does the earth as their mustaqarr mean?", "turns_on": "Whether mustaqarr is a place or action, and whether its scope includes burial; Ibn Ashur and al-Alusi give explicit objections to narrower or temporal readings.", "positions": [{"id": "7:24/q17/p1", "position": "A place of earthly dwelling and stability during life.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari calls the earth a spread-out resting place; Abu al-Aliya and al-Rabi link it to the earth made a bed in 2:22. Al-Biqa'i says the whole earth, including plains. Al-Mawardi and al-Nasafi allow a place noun, while Ibn Ashur identifies a mimetic verbal noun denoting remaining and cites 6:67 and 6:98; al-Alusi also allows the act of settling. Study Quran refers to 6:98. Ibn Ashur objects to graves because enjoyment follows and jinn or devils are not buried in earth."}, {"id": "7:24/q17/p2", "position": "The graves beneath the earth are the place of settlement.", "reasons": "Reports attribute this to Ibn Abbas, with Ibn Masud and al-Suddi agreeing in one transmission. Ibn Ashur rejects the burial reading because the clause also promises enjoyment and because jinn and devils are not buried in the earth."}, {"id": "7:24/q17/p3", "position": "Settlement covers life on the surface and residence beneath it after death.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari and Ibn Atiyya insist on the general scope and cite 77:25–26, earth containing the living and dead. Ibn Abbas is also reported to say both above and beneath the earth. Al-Alusi says grave dwelling can count as being in earth. Al-Durr's Jewish scholar adds the womb and final abode, Paradise or Hell, to the stages of human settlement."}, {"id": "7:24/q17/p4", "position": "Mustaqarr can describe the act or state of settling, rather than a physical place.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi contrasts the verbal act with Abu Salih's place gloss. Al-Nasafi says stability or place of stability; al-Alusi says settling or a place. Ibn Ashur's mimetic verbal noun denotes remaining or staying."}, {"id": "7:24/q17/p5", "position": "It may signify dominion established on earth and permission to use it.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi offers this meaning but calls it less apparent."}, {"id": "7:24/q17/p6", "position": "It could mean a period of settlement.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi rejects this because a temporal sense would repeat the subsequent 'until a time.'"}]}
{"id": "7:24/q18", "question": "What is the earthly matāʿ promised here?", "turns_on": "Whether the promise of enjoyment includes everyone addressed or is directed especially to Iblis.", "positions": [{"id": "7:24/q18/p1", "position": "Temporary worldly enjoyment, benefits, and sustenance for use.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi calls it worldly goods and benefits; al-Nasafi livelihood; Ibn Atiyya enjoyment and acquisition of benefit, mainly during life though a grave stay might somehow count. Ibn Ashur says the noun can denote passing pleasures or the useful things themselves and cites 4:102. Study Quran contrasts it with lasting reward or punishment of the Hereafter, citing 16:80, 2:36, 3:14, 4:77, 9:38, 10:70, 13:26, 20:131, 28:60, 40:39 and 42:36."}, {"id": "7:24/q18/p2", "position": "The temporary enjoyment is directed specifically to Iblis, although earthly dwelling is general.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayri distinguishes the scope of the two promises."}]}
{"id": "7:24/q19", "question": "How is the phrase 'on earth' attached grammatically?", "turns_on": "The attachment of 'on earth' and how the second nominal clause joins the first.", "positions": [{"id": "7:24/q19/p1", "position": "The earth clause is coordinated with the preceding enmity clause.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur treats the statement about settlement as joined to the statement that some are enemies to others."}, {"id": "7:24/q19/p2", "position": "The prepositional phrase attaches to enjoyment, to both enjoyment and settlement by attraction, or to an omitted adjective of enjoyment.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports these alternative syntactic attachments without selecting one."}]}
{"id": "7:24/q20", "question": "How long does earthly settlement and enjoyment last?", "turns_on": "Whether the addressees are viewed individually or collectively, and whether hin supplies a precise endpoint or only an indefinite interval.", "positions": [{"id": "7:24/q20/p1", "position": "Until each being's appointed lifespan ends in death.", "reasons": "Al-Suddi glosses provision as sustenance until death; Ibn Abbas through Ikrima glosses the term as life. Al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi, Bursevi, and Ibn Ashur likewise tie it to individual life; Ibn Ashur says this divinely determined term ends both settled existence and enjoyment, and is neither favor nor punishment. Ibn Kathir says terms are decreed and recorded in the first book; Muqatil gives Iblis a special term until the first trumpet."}, {"id": "7:24/q20/p2", "position": "Collectively the term extends until the Hour or the world's end, while individual enjoyment ends at death.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya explicitly distinguishes collective from individual duration; al-Biqa'i says lifespans expire and then the world ends. Al-Tabari and al-Mawardi identify the world's end, and Ibn Abbas names the Day of Resurrection. Al-Alusi reports death or resurrection as endpoints and allows 'for you' to refer collectively to humankind. Muqatil distinguishes ordinary lifetimes from Iblis's first-trumpet term."}, {"id": "7:24/q20/p3", "position": "The term lasts until arrival at Paradise or Hell.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas gives the final destinations as the end of provision."}, {"id": "7:24/q20/p4", "position": "Hin denotes an indefinite period, long or short, whose exact limit is not specified by the word itself.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari cites a poem about 'a time, no time'; al-Mawardi says the period can be long or short, usually suggesting long duration, and cites a poem. Ikrima calls it an unapprehended endpoint. Ibn Atiyya calls the time unspecified in Arabic usage; Ibn Ashur says its duration varies by kind and individual."}]}
{"id": "7:24/q21", "question": "What happened when Adam's earthly life ended?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:24/q21/p1", "position": "Angels washed, shrouded, and buried Adam in Serendib and taught his descendants burial practice.", "reasons": "Thabit al-Bunani reports that near death Eve circled the gathered angels and Adam told her to leave them, saying his fate came through her; the angels also perfumed him."}]}
{"id": "7:24/q22", "question": "Why were Adam and Eve sent to earth after repentance?", "turns_on": "How accepted repentance relates to the continued descent: punishment, planned trial, moral development, or providential spiritual gain.", "positions": [{"id": "7:24/q22/p1", "position": "Earth was appointed as the arena of a trial against Satan; Paradise becomes the reward for success.", "reasons": "Islahi says God's acceptance of repentance did not end the divinely planned contest; he cites the Adam sequence in 2:30–39. Kur'an Yolu cites 2:37 for accepted repentance and says earth became the place of testing. Al-Biqa'i calls earth an abode of struggle and urges constant vigilance, guided by reason and revelation, even after repentance. Thalabi describes living, dying and rising there."}, {"id": "7:24/q22/p2", "position": "The fall enabled freely chosen moral action, repentance and growth.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu says the first innocence was instinctive and lacked moral value; the tree's prohibition introduced choice, followed by wrongdoing, recognition, pardon and the capacity to choose goodness consciously. Study Quran says the fall manifests divine forgiveness and human humility and repentance, yielding a perfection otherwise unavailable."}, {"id": "7:24/q22/p3", "position": "The descent providentially enabled earthly vicegerency and nearness to God through exile.", "reasons": "Study Quran attributes this merciful interpretation to some Sufis and quotes Ibn Ata Allah: disobedience that breeds humility and need is better than obedience that breeds pride. Al-Qushayri says Adam lost his honored abode but retained virtue, citing God's choosing him in 20:122."}, {"id": "7:24/q22/p4", "position": "Adam and Eve's sin caused their expulsion and shaped humanity's fate.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu cites 2:36, 2:38 and 20:123, observes that the Torah narrates additional hardships absent from the Quran, and still describes repentance as accepted in 2:37."}]}
{"id": "7:24/q23", "question": "What does the descent teach about Adam's and Iblis's standing?", "turns_on": "How Adam's lapse relates to his preserved rank and prophethood, in contrast with Iblis's irreversible fall.", "positions": [{"id": "7:24/q23/p1", "position": "Adam lost his honored place but retained virtue and received mercy; Iblis fell in state and rank without recovery.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayri cites God's later choosing Adam in 20:122 and contrasts Adam's change of abode with Iblis's fall into curse. Bursevi, reporting al-Qushayri, says Adam's loss of garments and ease after one sin warns those committing many sins; a Hafiz couplet expresses longing for reunion while destiny binds the soul to separation. Bursevi adds that divine decree governs prophets and saints."}, {"id": "7:24/q23/p2", "position": "Adam's grave sin preceded his prophethood.", "reasons": "Al-Razi says this resolves the theological difficulty raised by the account, which he had discussed in al-Ba

{"id": "7:24/q24", "question": "What inward lessons are drawn from Adam's descent?", "turns_on": "The distinct symbolic lessons Bursevi draws from loss, knowledge and surrender.", "positions": [{"id": "7:24/q24/p1", "position": "Outward descent can be followed by spiritual ascent through love, loss and unveiling.", "reasons": "Bursevi says Adam ate from the tree of love, endured separation, and was promised discovery after loss. He warns against the tree of mere knowledge without direct witnessing: its owner remains veiled from reality, while God may complete a seeker's journey in the postmortem isthmus."}, {"id": "7:24/q24/p2", "position": "The seeker should relinquish self-directed planning and submit to divine decree.", "reasons": "Bursevi reads prayer's standing as primordial surrender, bowing as submission to eternal ordering, and prostration as effacement of both; he also says decree governs prophets and saints."}]}
{"id": "7:24/q25", "question": "What are the conditions and protections of earthly life?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:24/q25/p1", "position": "Earthly life alternates hardship and ease, good and evil, life and death, victory and loss, with means of protection from harm.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayri says God conceals people from visible causes of harm and equips them with benefits to ward off many harms."}]}
{"id": "7:24/q26", "question": "Do this verse and 6:38 show that animals share human religious obligations?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:24/q26/p1", "position": "No; that inference from the combined verses is strained.", "reasons": "Al-Burhan rejects the argument that animals bear the same religious obligations as humans, despite its appeal to 7:24 and 6:38."}]}
{"id": "7:24/q27", "question": "How does this verse connect with the surrounding Quranic account?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:24/q27/p1", "position": "It continues the Adam narrative and parallels the descent account in al-Baqara and 20:123.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisi, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan refer readers to prior treatment in al-Baqara; Abu Hayyan names 2:36. Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Kathir cite 20:123 for Adam–Iblis enmity. Kur'an Yolu links 2:36, 2:38 and 20:123; Study Quran places 7:24 within verses 11–27 on creation, temptation and expulsion. Ibn Atiyya says he abbreviated extra reports because the present wording does not demand them."}]}
{"id": "7:25/q01", "question": "Why is قال repeated without a conjunction?", "turns_on": "Whether the second utterance explains the first, begins a new or emphasized speech, reflects a discourse shift, follows omitted speech, or simply follows accepted narrative usage.", "positions": [{"id": "7:25/q01/p1", "position": "The new sentence explains the preceding statement, so Arabic leaves it uncoordinated.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān says successive sentences normally take coordination unless the second interprets the first. He identifies the earlier statement as the earthly settlement and provision of 7:24."}, {"id": "7:25/q01/p2", "position": "The repeated قال marks a fresh utterance or emphasizes the earthly-life decree.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī gives renewed speech or emphasis. Ibn ʿĀshūr reports Abū al-Suʿūd's emphasis explanation."}, {"id": "7:25/q01/p3", "position": "The absence of a conjunction is permissible Arabic narration, though it departs from expected coordination.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī says adding wāw would also be grammatical, illustrating this with Zayd speaking to ʿAmr. Ibn ʿĀshūr notes that the same speaker and purpose would lead one to expect coordination; he says many leading exegetes, including al-Zamakhsharī, leave the absence unexplained, perhaps as a storytelling convention."}, {"id": "7:25/q01/p4", "position": "A change in the kind of discourse can account for repeated قال.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr reports Ibn ʿArafa's explanation of the analogous 7:140 after 7:138: first comes rejection of idolatry, then an argument against it. Al-Khafājī gives the same explanation without attribution."}, {"id": "7:25/q01/p5", "position": "Unreported intervening speech separates the two utterances.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr reports this suggestion from Abū al-Suʿūd, who compares 15:56–57 and 17:61–62. Ibn ʿĀshūr rejects the inference because a report of speech need not be exhaustive or continuous."}]}
{"id": "7:25/q02", "question": "Who receives this decree?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:25/q02/p1", "position": "Adam, his wife, and their descendants, extending the address to humanity.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls this probable because a new قال introduces the decree. Al-Biqāʿī and Elmalılı discuss its force for human beings or the human species generally."}]}
{"id": "7:25/q03", "question": "What do فيها and منها refer to?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:25/q03/p1", "position": "They refer to the earth of this world, already named as humanity's abode in 7:24.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās specifies this world's earth for living. Al-Wāḥidī derives the pronoun from the preceding earthly abode in 7:24. Ibn al-Jawzī identifies the referent of فيها as earth. Al-Qurṭubī extends the earth referent to all the pronouns."}]}
{"id": "7:25/q04", "question": "What is meant by living فيها?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:25/q04/p1", "position": "People live their worldly lives on earth until death, within the earthly settlement God decreed.", "reasons": "Muqātil and al-Ṭabarī specify the span of each lifespan. Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls the decree irrevocable. Abū Ḥayyān connects it to 7:24's settlement and provision. Al-Biqāʿī adds outward and inward life of bodies and souls, first and again on this earth, excluding another earthly realm. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī distinguishes each person or community's lifespan here from humanity's wider span of earthly provision, ending at extinction or resurrection."}]}
{"id": "7:25/q05", "question": "What is meant by dying فيها?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:25/q05/p1", "position": "People die on earth and are buried in it when their earthly lives end.", "reasons": "Muqātil ties death to the end of one's appointed lifespan. Al-Kalbī, al-Baghawī, Ibn Kathīr, and Bursawī explicitly mention burial. Al-Biqāʿī says death concerns the person as a whole but the soul retains a connection to the body, allowing answers to grave angels and bodily pleasure or pain."}]}
{"id": "7:25/q06", "question": "What relation does death have to life?", "turns_on": "Whether death is understood as nonbeing or as a contrary to life.", "positions": [{"id": "7:25/q06/p1", "position": "Life and death are contraries.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān calls this the sounder account."}, {"id": "7:25/q06/p2", "position": "If death is nonbeing, death and life are privation and possession.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān states this conditional account while preferring the contrary account."}]}
{"id": "7:25/q07", "question": "Why does life precede death in this verse?", "turns_on": "The addressees' lived sequence versus the meanings served by a death-first order in other contexts.", "positions": [{"id": "7:25/q07/p1", "position": "The addressees, whether Adam and Eve or living people generally, live before they die.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān gives both scopes of address. He explicitly raises this ordering question; his discussion of the contrary sequence in the command to Mary has no answer in the excerpt."}, {"id": "7:25/q07/p2", "position": "A death-first sequence elsewhere can emphasize prior nonexistence or the world's transient destination.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān says death can be prior as nonexistence or the final destination of worldly life; such ordering can disparage the transient world and direct desire beyond death, citing 23:15. This explains the alternate order rather than replacing the life-first explanation here."}]}
{"id": "7:25/q08", "question": "How is تُخْرَجُونَ read, and how does the reading express agency?", "turns_on": "Whether the verb is active with fatḥa on the prefix and ḍamma on rāʾ, or passive with ḍamma on the prefix and fatḥa on rāʾ; reader assignments and related passages provide the evidence.", "positions": [{"id": "7:25/q08/p1", "position": "The active form means 'you come out,' making the people the grammatical subject.", "reasons": "Al-Fārisī cites the agreed active 30:25, the people as subject of ينسلون in 36:51, and 7:29's return imagery. Al-Jishumī says the action is attributed to people; QIRAAT-ER takes this as autonomous emergence rather than divine extraction. Reports assign the active here to Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī, also Khalaf or Kūfans other than ʿĀṣim; Ibn ʿĀmir, Ibn Dhakwān, and Yaʿqūb are reported to agree here. Reports differ in detail about corresponding forms in al-Rūm, al-Zukhruf, and al-Jāthiya: al-Fārisī, al-Jishumī, al-Baghawī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Bayḍāwī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn, and Ibn al-Jazarī specify differing scopes and exceptions, including 30:19 or 30:25, 43:11, 45:35, and 70:43."}, {"id": "7:25/q08/p2", "position": "The passive form means 'you are brought out,' leaving the grammatical agent unnamed.", "reasons": "Al-Fārisī supports it with مخرجون in 23:35 and God's bringing out the dead in 7:57. Al-Jishumī contrasts its unnamed agent with the active form. Reports assign it here to Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim, or the remaining Seven; al-Samīn says both readings are clear. Reports give related passive patterns and exceptions at 30:19, 30:25, 43:11, 45:35, and 70:43; Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Ibn al-Jawzī call the active forms at 30:25 and 70:43 agreed exceptions."}]}
{"id": "7:25/q09", "question": "What does emergence from the earth entail?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:25/q09/p1", "position": "People are raised from earth or its graves, alive for the resurrection, gathering, judgment, and recompense.", "reasons": "Muqātil and al-Ṭabarī place it on Resurrection Day; al-Ṭabarī explicitly says God brings and gathers people alive. Al-Kalbī and al-Baghawī specify graves. Ibn ʿAṭiy

ya calls it God's irrevocable decree and says He restores first creation. Al-Bayḍāwī says judgment; al-Nasafī and Abū Ḥayyān say reward or punishment, the latter comparing 20:55. Ibn Kathīr says first and last are gathered and repaid for deeds. Al-Biqāʿī adds bodily and spiritual return from dust and restoration of rights as God's justice. Elmalılı says this establishes the human species on earth; Iṣlāḥī says God then shows people their gains, losses, and success."}]}
{"id": "7:25/q10", "question": "From which earth are people raised, and where are they taken afterward?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:25/q10/p1", "position": "They rise from this same earth; God then destroys it and moves them by a blast to al-Sāhira.", "reasons": "Al-Jubbāʾī cites 79:14 for the subsequent move to the land called al-Sāhira."}]}
{"id": "7:25/q11", "question": "Does resurrection restore bodily existence after death?", "turns_on": "Whether souls retain bodily connection and return bodily, or leave bodies permanently for celestial existence.", "positions": [{"id": "7:25/q11/p1", "position": "Yes; body and soul remain connected in the grave and emerge together from the earth for requital.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says the dead answer grave angels and feel pleasure or pain, then return from dust as body and soul; restoration of rights manifests divine justice. He rejects the philosophers' denial of later bodily attachment."}, {"id": "7:25/q11/p2", "position": "No; souls leave bodies for celestial beings or realms, without later bodily attachment or resurrection.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī attributes this to transmigrationist philosophers and rejects it."}]}
{"id": "7:25/q12", "question": "What is the inward reading of living, dying, and emerging?", "turns_on": "Whether the stages signify gnosis, ignorance, and decree, or the seeker's movement through love and spiritual discipline to reality.", "positions": [{"id": "7:25/q12/p1", "position": "One lives by gnosis, dies by ignorance, and emerges into prior decrees and governing judgments.", "reasons": "Al-Sulamī reports this from an unnamed interpreter."}, {"id": "7:25/q12/p2", "position": "One lives in love and sincere, patient servitude, dies while seeking the Real through Sharīʿa and ṭarīqa, then emerges into reality.", "reasons": "Bursawī urges steadfast waiting for relief. He cites a Prophetic report that people die as they live and are raised as they die. His Persian verses commend striving for love and portray night prayer and dawn weeping as guidance through darkness."}]}
{"id": "7:25/q13", "question": "How does the decree connect with the surrounding Adam narrative?", "turns_on": "Whether the connection stressed is the preceding earthly settlement or the narrative's return to the afterlife.", "positions": [{"id": "7:25/q13/p1", "position": "It spells out the earlier earthly settlement and provision in 7:24.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī links the pronoun to the prior earthly abode. Abū Ḥayyān says earthly life lasts until death. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī distinguishes each person's or community's life and death from humanity's wider period of provision; he treats the new قال as introducing the decree. Elmalılı and Kur'an Yolu describe the establishment and spread of the human species on earth."}, {"id": "7:25/q13/p2", "position": "Its resurrection promise closes Adam's story by returning to the afterlife and humanity's ultimate fate.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says the story ends where its afterlife message began. Study Quran describes 7:11–27 as Adam's creation, temptation, and expulsion and says the life–death–resurrection sequence recalls ultimate fate. Bursawī says Adam took comfort in an inferred return to Paradise."}]}
{"id": "7:25/q14", "question": "What does Adam's fall in this account teach about sin, decree, and guidance?", "turns_on": "Which moral or theological implication is drawn from the fall: the timing of Adam's sin, warning under decree, need for guidance, or the emergence of accountable freedom.", "positions": [{"id": "7:25/q14/p1", "position": "Adam's grave sin occurred before his prophethood.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says the account, as explained in al-Baqara, implies grave sin and resolves the difficulty by placing it before prophethood."}, {"id": "7:25/q14/p2", "position": "Even an honored person can lose ease after one sin; divine decree governs prophets and saints alike.", "reasons": "Bursawī reports al-Qushayrī's warning from Adam's lost garments and ease: many sins are more alarming. He also reports Ḥāfiẓ's couplet about longing for union while destiny binds the soul to separation, and himself states that decree governs all."}, {"id": "7:25/q14/p3", "position": "Adam's temptation illustrates human weakness and the continuing need for prophetic guidance.", "reasons": "Asad connects appetite, vanity, and false self-interest to human susceptibility, citing the temptation and fall at 7:16, 7:18, 7:19, and 7:25."}, {"id": "7:25/q14/p4", "position": "The move after the first sin marks humanity's rise to free moral accountability and conscious choice of good.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu says humans can err and repent; it describes the move as moral rise rather than moral decline."}]}
{"id": "7:25/q15", "question": "What ancillary observations appear in these notes without an explicit application to 7:25?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:25/q15/p1", "position": "The source excerpts include a lexical note on riyāshan and a separate note about an omitted vocative at 30:23.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda equates riyāshan and rīshan and gives visible clothing, adornment, equipment including saddle trappings, and abundance or livelihood. Al-Samīn reports Makkī's point that omitting yā in the prayer at 30:23 exalts God and removes the imperative-like force of the vocative. Neither note states an application to the wording of 7:25."}]}
{"id": "7:57/q01", "question": "How are wind and its verse description read and understood?", "turns_on": "The readings vary between singular and plural wind and between bāʾ for glad tidings and nūn for spreading, revival, or fragrance; grammatical analyses also vary.", "positions": [{"id": "7:57/q01/p1", "position": "Plural winds with bāʾ describe bearers of good news of rain.", "reasons": "ʿĀṣim is repeatedly named; 30:46 is cited by al-Ṭabarī, al-Baghawī, al-Ṭabrisī, and others. The form is explained as plural bashīr or bashīra, a lightened plural, or a verbal noun; Ibn ʿAbbās says people rejoice at the winds. Al-Ṭabarī accepts its meaning but does not favor the reading."}, {"id": "7:57/q01/p2", "position": "Plural winds with nūn describe winds spread out from different directions.", "reasons": "Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, Hijazis and Basrans are widely named for nushuran; Ibn ʿĀmir and others lighten shīn. Some derive a plural of nashūr or nāshir, an active or passive form, or a verbal noun. Abū ʿUbayda describes dispersal; al-Farrāʾ and Imruʾ al-Qays support gentle fragrant wind; other poets support life and revival. Al-Ṭabarī accepts both regional nūn forms; Abū Ḥātim favors rounded vowels and Abū ʿUbayd favors the Kufan form."}, {"id": "7:57/q01/p3", "position": "Singular wind is a valid collective reading, although several sources favor plural agreement and associate plural winds with mercy.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr, Ḥamza, and al-Kisāʾī are named. Al-Fārisī, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Rāzī, and al-Samīn cite 103:2–3 and poetry for singular form with plural sense. Al-Fārisī and Abū ʿAlī prefer formal plural agreement; Ibn ʿAṭiyya favors plural because mercy winds are separate and punitive winds one force, but explains generic singular and ship/Solomon exceptions. Prophetic supplication asks for plural winds. Rīḥ has root wāw; riyāḥ is abundance plural and arwāḥ paucity plural."}]}
